planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, giving the tree room to grow into a tall, upright form reminiscent of the native American parent.

directions: Named for Dr. Arthur H. Graves, who began crossing American and Asian chestnuts on his family's land in Hamden, Connecticut starting in 1930 while curator at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, this cultivar is a backcross of a Chinese-American hybrid onto American chestnut. The Hamden land was later sold to the Sleeping Giant Park Association and conveyed to the state, with Graves's chestnut plantings preserved there as the Sleeping Giant Chestnut Plantation. This backcross tree, developed jointly through USDA and Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station work, helped jump-start the modern American Chestnut Foundation backcross breeding program decades later. Plant it with an unrelated chestnut cultivar nearby for cross-pollination, in deep, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, and expect some susceptibility to blight cankers compared with pure Chinese selections since resistance in these early backcross lines is only partial.
sources: The Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (Cultivars of Chestnut)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this selection traces to a single blight-surviving American chestnut and benefits from good air flow to limit canker development.

directions: Carpentar traces to an Ohio man of that name who, in the early 1950s, found a mature, apparently healthy American chestnut standing in a grove of blight-killed trees and, after repeated attempts to inoculate it with blight failed to produce disease, sent budwood to breeder Dr. Robert T. Dunstan. Dunstan grafted and cross-pollinated the tree with the Chinese chestnut selections Kuling, Meiling, and Nanking, and the resulting hybrids, first bearing around 1962, became the foundation of the whole Dunstan chestnut line. As a named selection from that original cross, Carpentar shows the blight tolerance and precocious bearing typical of early Dunstan hybrids. Give it full sun, deep well-drained soil, and a second unrelated cultivar for pollination, and expect nuts within a few years of planting a grafted tree.
sources: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (Cultivars of Chestnut)

common_name: Heritage Chestnut (Patented American-Form Dunstan Hybrid, USPP6674)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; expect the first light crop within three to four years of grafting.

directions: Heritage is a patented Dunstan-line selection (U.S. Plant Patent PP6,674, Robert D. Wallace) descended from the same 1953 cross of a surviving American chestnut with the Chinese selections Kuling, Meiling, and Nanking that produced the broader Dunstan hybrid group. It grows with an upright, straight-trunked, timber-like habit unusually close to a pure American chestnut, bearing medium-sized, elongated, sweet dark-brown nuts with pointed stylar tips, two to three to a burr, on a light but dependable annual schedule in late September to early October. Burrs tend to split and drop their nuts cleanly on the tree, easing harvest. The original patent documented no instance of blight infection over 25 years of observation, though as with any orchard planting, cross-pollination with a second unrelated cultivar is required for good nut set.
sources: USPTO Plant Patent PP6,674 (Robert D. Wallace)
Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (Cultivars of Chestnut)

common_name: Mountaineer Chestnut (West Virginia American-Form Blight-Resistant Hybrid)
scientific_name: Castanea dentata x ((crenata x dentata) x mollissima) 'Mountaineer'

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun on a site with good air movement; nuts typically drop earlier than those of pure American chestnut, in late summer to early fall.

directions: Mountaineer was produced from a 1998 controlled cross at a West Virginia orchard, pairing a partially blight-resistant wild American chestnut designated WV-1 with a Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station hybrid pollen parent, yielding a tree estimated at roughly five-eighths American ancestry with the remainder Chinese and Japanese. The goal was to combine the tall, rapid-growing, visually American habit and sweet flavor of the native species with meaningfully better blight tolerance than a pure American tree can offer. Nuts run slightly larger than wild American chestnuts and drop earlier in the season, in early September rather than October. Give it full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and plant a second unrelated cultivar nearby since chestnuts need cross-pollination to bear well.
sources: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (Cultivars of Chestnut)
The American Chestnut Foundation, West Virginia Chapter

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this selection tolerates some blight exposure better than pure American chestnut but still benefits from monitoring for cankers.

directions: Sheryl was the first named selection at a West Virginia chestnut orchard, resulting from a 1990 controlled cross using a wild American chestnut (WV-1) as the seed parent and a Chinese chestnut growing as a lawn tree in Philippi, West Virginia as the pollen parent. Its nuts land in size between the smaller American and larger Chinese parents, and are notably uniform in shape with good, reliable flavor. Blight resistance is intermediate, meaningfully better than a pure American chestnut though not as strong as a pure Chinese tree. Grow it in full sun and deep, well-drained soil with an unrelated cultivar nearby for pollination, and watch young grafts for canker during the establishment years.
sources: The American Chestnut Foundation, West Virginia Chapter
